1345.title: Lourdes
1345.hook: the spring, the sick, and a medical bureau that investigates claimed cures
1345.howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to the grotto at Lourdes, where the sick are given the first place in processions, pilgrims drink and wash in the spring water, and a medical office examines reported cures before any bishop judges them.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the tilma of Guadalupe: a woman praying before the sun, with a band at her waist. Your line was she carries him.

On a kitchen shelf sits a small plastic bottle shaped like Mary, with a blue cap for a crown. Somebody's aunt brought it home from France, filled from a row of taps by a river. Nobody drinks it casually. It gets a drop on a sick child's forehead, or a sip before surgery. The water comes from a spring in a grotto at Lourdes, in the foothills of the Pyrenees, and it draws the sick from far away. And beside the grotto is something you might not expect at a shrine: an office full of doctors whose job is to be skeptical.
screen: `A BOTTLE SHAPED LIKE MARY.` → `WATER FROM A GROTTO IN FRANCE.` → `AND AN OFFICE FULL OF DOCTORS.`

segments.voice: You met Bernadette at this grotto back in year one. First, the spring. Tradition says the lady told Bernadette to drink from the spring and wash in it, and there was no spring, only mud. She dug with her hands, and the water came. Water and washing matter in the Gospels too. Jesus puts clay on the eyes of a man born blind and says, in the Douay-Rheims, "Go, wash in the pool of Siloe." The man washes and comes back seeing. Lourdes stands in that line. Second, who goes first. At Lourdes the sick aren't kept out of sight. Volunteers push their wheelchairs and stretchers to the front of the processions, to the baths, to the grotto. The people the world hurries past are guests of honor. Third, the doctors. When someone claims a cure, the shrine's medical office examines it. Was the illness real and serious? Was the cure sudden, complete and lasting? Can medicine explain it? Only if a cure passes all of that does it go to the healed person's own bishop, who decides whether to call it a miracle. The bar is high, and the process slow. Fourth, the water itself. The shrine says it's ordinary spring water. Catholics treat it as a sign: of washing, of trust, of asking. Sick pilgrims can go home no better in body. Some say they came back changed anyway, less alone and less afraid, and they return to push someone else's wheelchair.

segments.voice: Picture the grotto at night: candles, a long line of wheelchairs, volunteers leaning on the handles. Bring in one sick person you know by name, set them in that line near the front, and stay with them a while. If you pray, say a Hail Mary for the sick at Lourdes and for them; if not, simply keep them company in your mind.
Lourdes. The French town where a spring rises in a grotto, the sick go first, and doctors test every claimed cure before a bishop will call it a miracle. Today's word.
Your line: the waters. Ordinary spring water, carried home as a sign. See you tomorrow.

1346.title: Fatima, simply
1346.hook: three children, a call to prayer, and the crowd's report of the sun in 1917
1346.howItsDone: Catholics who honor Our Lady of Fatima pray the rosary, often daily, as the children reported she asked; pilgrims visit the shrine at Fatima in Portugal, and her feast is kept in May.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Lourdes: a spring dug from mud, the sick at the front of the line, and doctors who test every claimed cure. Your line was the waters.

Type the word Fatima into a search bar. Secrets. Prophecies. Countdown videos. Arguments about what was hidden and who hid it. Underneath all that noise is a much quieter story: shepherd children in the hills of Portugal, a lady who asked them to pray, and a crowd in a muddy field that later told what they saw in the sky. Today's title has a second word, and it's the important one: simply. The secrets get set down, and the question is what the children were actually asked to do.
screen: `SECRETS, PROPHECIES, COUNTDOWNS.` → `UNDERNEATH, A QUIET STORY.` → `FATIMA, SIMPLY.`

segments.voice: You've met these children before on this path. First, the children. Lucia and her younger cousins, Francisco and Jacinta, were watching sheep near the village of Fatima when, by their account, a lady brighter than the sun appeared to them, and came back over the following months. What she asked wasn't complicated: pray the rosary every day, pray for sinners, turn back to God. The children took it seriously in a child's way. Francisco would slip off to pray alone; Jacinta offered small sacrifices for others. Both are now honored as saints. Second, the sun. At the last visit, a large crowd came, in the rain. People later said the sun seemed to spin and dance and plunge toward them, and that their soaked clothes were suddenly dry. Accounts differ, and some people present reported nothing unusual. The Church approved the apparitions, and, as you heard three days ago, no Catholic is required to believe them. Third, the message is old. Without the drama, Fatima says what Jesus said when he first began to preach, in the Douay-Rheims of Mark's Gospel: "The time is accomplished, and the kingdom of God is at hand: repent, and believe the gospel." Repent is a call to turn around: not a new teaching, but the one Jesus opened with, repeated by children in a field. Fourth, the rosary. The daily request wasn't a crusade or a secret code. It was beads in a pocket, prayer the size of a few minutes. That's Fatima, simply: pray, and turn around, and start again tomorrow.
screen: `CHILDREN ASKED TO PRAY.` · `THE SUN, AS THE CROWD TOLD IT.` · `AN OLD MESSAGE: TURN AROUND.` · `BEADS IN A POCKET.` · then, large: `REPENT, AND BELIEVE THE GOSPEL.`

segments.voice: A decade of the rosary is one Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be. If you pray, say one now, slowly, on your fingers if you have no beads; if you don't, count ten slow breaths on your fingers, and with each, name one thing you'd like to turn away from, or turn toward.
Fatima. The Portuguese village where shepherd children said a lady asked for daily prayer and conversion, and where a crowd reported a sign in the sun. Today's word.
Your line: pray and repent. An old message, carried by children in a field. Until tomorrow.

1347.title: Knock (1879)
1347.hook: a silent apparition in the rain in an Irish village
1347.howItsDone: Catholics make pilgrimages to the shrine at Knock in County Mayo, Ireland, where the gable wall of the old parish church is kept as a chapel; pilgrims pray the rosary there and come for Mass and confession.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Fatima, simply: children asked to pray every day and turn back to God. Your line was pray and repent.

It's a wet evening in a small village in the west of Ireland, and it's raining hard. A woman walking past the parish church stops. She sees figures, she'll later say, at the gable wall, standing in a soft light a little above the grass. She runs for others. Neighbors come, old people and children. They stand in the downpour and look, and kneel, and someone starts the rosary. The figures don't move toward them. Nobody calls out, nobody asks for anything, nobody gives a message. People stay a long time, soaked, praying, watching. And then it's over.
screen: `RAIN ON A VILLAGE CHURCH.` → `FIGURES AT THE GABLE WALL.` → `NOBODY SAYS A WORD.`

segments.voice: First, the silence. Lourdes had a lady who spoke to Bernadette; Fatima had requests for the children. At Knock, by the witnesses' accounts, no one spoke at all. For a Church that has heard so many words, that's a striking thing to keep. Second, who was there. The witnesses described Mary, crowned, her hands raised and her eyes lifted, as if in prayer. Beside her, Joseph, his head bowed toward her. On her other side, a figure they took to be John the Evangelist, dressed like a bishop and holding an open book. And in the middle, an altar, with a cross and a lamb standing on it. Third, the lamb. In the Apocalypse, the book John is said to have written, he sees in heaven, in the Douay-Rheims, "a Lamb standing as it were slain." For Christians, the Lamb is Christ: wounded, and alive. Some readers see the whole vision as a picture of the Mass, with Mary, Joseph and John gathered around the altar, saying nothing, because the one in the middle is the point. Fourth, why silence speaks. Knock was a poor village in a country that had known famine and hard years. What came wasn't a lecture or a warning. It was company, in the rain. The prophet Habacuc has a line for it: "But the Lord is in his holy temple: let all the earth keep silence before him." At Knock, the earth did.
screen: `NO ONE SPOKE.` · `MARY, JOSEPH, JOHN.` · `A LAMB ON THE ALTAR.` · `SILENCE AS COMPANY.` · then, large: `LET ALL THE EARTH KEEP SILENCE BEFORE HIM.`

segments.voice: No words today, not even inside; if a thought starts talking, let it trail off, the way a conversation stops when someone points at the sky. Think of the people at the gable wall, kneeling in the rain, watching: you don't have to see anything, just be someone who stays. If you pray, let this be prayer without a single word in it; if not, let it be honest quiet.
Knock. The Irish village where, by the witnesses' accounts, Mary, Joseph and John stood beside an altar with a lamb, in the rain, and not one word was spoken. Today's word.
Your line: the silent apparition. Company, without a single word. One thousand three hundred forty-seven days now.

1348.title: Kibeho (Rwanda)
1348.hook: visions in the 1980s that were later read as warnings before the genocide
1348.howItsDone: Catholics honor Our Lady of Kibeho at the Shrine of Our Lady of Sorrows in Kibeho, Rwanda, where pilgrims pray, often using the rosary of the Seven Sorrows the visionaries said Mary asked for, and remember those killed in the genocide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Knock: a vision in the Irish rain where no one said a word. Your line was the silent apparition.

Nyina wa Jambo. In Kinyarwanda, the language of Rwanda, that means Mother of the Word. It's the name schoolgirls at a boarding school in the village of Kibeho said a lady gave herself when she appeared to them. Their classmates mocked them. Teachers doubted them. Crowds came to watch them in their visions, some believers, others not. And among the things the young women described were scenes so dark that, years later, people in Rwanda looked back at them and shivered.
screen: `NYINA WA JAMBO.` → `SCHOOLGIRLS, DOUBTED AND MOCKED.` → `SCENES PEOPLE LATER LOOKED BACK AT.`

segments.voice: Begin with the name. Mother of the Word points to the opening of John's Gospel, where the Word is with God in the beginning, and then, in the Douay-Rheims, "the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." To call Mary Mother of the Word is to say who she is entirely through her son. Then the message. By the young women's accounts, the lady asked for prayer and conversion, for hearts turned back to God before it was too late. She asked them to pray the rosary of the Seven Sorrows, which walks through Mary's griefs. Then the darkness. In one vision, by the accounts, they saw terrible things: rivers of blood, people killing one another, bodies left unburied. They wept as they described it. Later, Rwanda went through the genocide against the Tutsi, and Kibeho itself became a place of killing. Afterward, people came to read those visions as warnings that had come before. No one is required to read them that way; it's a reading made looking back. The Church studied the visions carefully and recognized some of them. Last, the sorrow. Kibeho today has a shrine to Our Lady of Sorrows, a place of pilgrimage and of mourning. Matthew's Gospel, telling of children killed in Bethlehem, borrows a prophet's line: "Rachel bewailing her children, and would not be comforted, because they are not." The Gospel doesn't explain that grief away, and a shrine of sorrows doesn't either.
screen: `MOTHER OF THE WORD.` · `PRAY, AND TURN BACK.` · `VISIONS READ AS WARNINGS.` · `A SHRINE OF SORROWS.` · then, large: `THE WORD WAS MADE FLESH.`

segments.voice: Hold Rwanda in mind, its hills, its villages, its people today, and then the ones who survived and still carry what they lost, the ones working slowly to live beside neighbors again, the ones never mourned by name. Don't hurry past the heaviness. If you pray, say a Hail Mary for Rwanda or pray one of the Seven Sorrows; if not, simply hold its people gently. And if this stirs a grief too heavy to hold, or you don't want to be alive, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.

1349.title: Vailankanni (India)
1349.hook: a coastal shrine of Our Lady of Good Health, loved by people of many religions
1349.howItsDone: Pilgrims come to the Basilica of Our Lady of Good Health at Vailankanni in Tamil Nadu, India, to pray for healing, some walking on their knees or offering small models of the part of the body they hope to see healed; people of other faiths visit and pray there too.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kibeho: visions in Rwanda, and a lady who called herself Mother of the Word. Your line was mother of the word.

On the beach, a woman in a yellow sari is making her way toward a white church on her knees. Behind her, a father carries a little boy whose head has just been shaved, an offering for a fever that broke. At a stall nearby, someone buys a small wax model of a leg, to leave at the altar for a knee that won't heal. Some pilgrims are Catholic, some Hindu, some Muslim. They've all come to the same shore in the south of India, to a mother they call Our Lady of Good Health.
screen: `ON HER KNEES TOWARD A WHITE CHURCH.` → `A WAX LEG FOR A BAD KNEE.` → `ONE SHORE, PILGRIMS OF MANY FAITHS.`

segments.voice: Start with the stories, which come from tradition rather than any record. Tradition says a boy carrying milk to a customer stopped to rest under a tree, and a beautiful lady holding a child asked him for milk for her son. He gave it, and arrived to find his pot still full. Another story tells of a lame boy selling buttermilk who was asked the same, gave, and stood up and walked. And sailors caught in a storm are said to have promised Mary a chapel if they reached land alive. They did, and they built it. What holds these stories together: a mother asking for something for her child, and people healed and kept safe. Next, the name. The Litany of Loreto calls Mary health of the sick, and Vailankanni gives her almost that title. People come carrying their bodies: bad backs, failing eyes, children who won't eat, babies long hoped for. They leave wax or metal models of the part that hurts, a kind of prayer you can hold in your hand. In Matthew's Gospel, a sick woman pushes through a crowd toward Jesus, thinking, in the Douay-Rheims: "If I shall touch only his garment, I shall be healed." She wanted to bring her body close. Last, the neighbors. The shrine's gates stand open, and people of other faiths come to pray there too, in their own ways. Catholics there don't check anyone at the door; they meet them as fellow pilgrims, all asking for the same plain thing.
screen: `A MOTHER ASKS FOR MILK.` · `HEALTH OF THE SICK.` · `BRINGING THE BODY CLOSE.` · `OPEN TO NEIGHBORS.` · then, large: `IF I SHALL TOUCH ONLY HIS GARMENT, I SHALL BE HEALED.`

segments.voice: Rest a few breaths on one part of your body that works without your asking, then on one part that hurts, without arguing with it. Now hold someone whose health is failing just as gently. If you pray, say a Hail Mary for them, or the litany's words, health of the sick, pray for us; if not, wish them well, by name.

1350.title: La Vang (Vietnam)
1350.hook: Catholics hiding from persecution in 1798 remember Mary appearing in the forest
1350.howItsDone: Catholics in Vietnam and abroad honor Our Lady of La Vang; pilgrims travel to the shrine at La Vang in central Vietnam to pray, and Vietnamese Catholic communities elsewhere keep images of her in their churches.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vailankanni: a shrine on India's coast where pilgrims bring their bodies' worries. Your line was our lady of good health.

A pot of leaves is boiling over a small fire, deep in a forest in the hills of central Vietnam. Around it sit families who have left their villages. They are Catholics, and in their country, at this time, being Catholic could cost you your home or your life. So they've come to the trees to hide. Some are sick with fever. There's no doctor, no medicine, and nowhere safer to go. At night they pray the rosary together, quietly. The leaves in that pot have a story, and Vietnamese Catholics still tell it.
screen: `A POT OF LEAVES OVER A FIRE.` → `CATHOLICS HIDING IN THE TREES.` → `SICK, WITH NOWHERE TO GO.`

segments.voice: First, the hiding. Tradition says that during a time of persecution, Catholics fled into the forest at La Vang. The Letter to the Hebrews describes believers like them, in the Douay-Rheims: "wandering in deserts, in mountains, and in dens, and in caves of the earth." A church without a building, praying under the trees. Second, the mother. Tradition says that as they prayed, a lady appeared among the branches, holding a child, with angels beside her. She didn't promise them their villages back, or that their persecutors would fall. She comforted them and told them what to do: gather the leaves from the trees around them and boil them as medicine for the sick. Third, the leaves. That small, practical instruction echoes the Bible's last chapter. In John's vision of the heavenly city, the tree of life grows by the river, and "the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations." At La Vang, by the people's memory, the healing came from the ordinary trees they were hiding under. In the story, heaven doesn't lift them out of the forest; it meets them in it. Fourth, the keeping. Tradition says the survivors remembered, and built a small chapel on the spot, and pilgrims still gather under the trees as those families did. Like every apparition, La Vang asks no one to believe it. What it hands on is a picture: a mother finding her children exactly where they were hiding.

1351.title: Consecration to Mary
1351.hook: John Paul II's motto was totally yours, from Montfort
1351.howItsDone: Some Catholics make a consecration to Jesus through Mary, often following Louis de Montfort's method of preparation, and some renew it each year; Pope John Paul II took Totus Tuus, from this tradition, as his motto.

segments.voice: Yesterday, La Vang: Catholics hiding in a Vietnamese forest, told to boil the leaves for healing. Your line was in the forest.

Bishops' coats of arms can get crowded: keys, lions, towers, a shell or two. When Karol Wojtyła became a bishop in Poland, his was nearly empty. A plain cross, a little off center. Beneath one arm of it, a capital M, for Mary, standing near the cross the way she stood near it on Calvary. And under the shield, two Latin words. He kept them when he became Pope John Paul the Second, under the same plain cross. Today's word is those two words.
screen: `A NEARLY EMPTY COAT OF ARMS.` → `A CROSS, AND AN M BENEATH IT.` → `TWO LATIN WORDS.`

segments.voice: First, the words. Totus tuus: totally yours. They're spoken to Mary, but they're not about her alone. Second, where he found them. You met Louis de Montfort earlier on this path: a French priest who wrote a book on what he called true devotion to Mary. Its center is an act Catholics call consecration: giving yourself entirely to Jesus, through Mary. Your prayers, your work, your days, all handed to her, so she can bring them to her son. Totus tuus comes out of that tradition. Third, a young man's worry. John Paul wrote that as a young man he had worried that loving Mary too much might crowd out Christ. Reading Montfort changed his mind. Devotion to Mary, done rightly, doesn't stop at her; it leads to Christ, the way a mother takes your hand and walks you to her son. Fourth, where it ends. Paul, writing to the Galatians, describes a life handed over so completely that it's no longer only his own. In the Douay-Rheims: "And I live, now not I; but Christ liveth in me." Consecration, in this tradition, aims there: Mary is the way in, and her son is the one it reaches. This week went to the places where Catholics remember her coming, from a spring at Lourdes to a forest at La Vang. Today it stays home, with two words a pope wore under a cross.

segments.voice: Walk through today in your mind, or tomorrow if today is nearly done: the first thing you'll do, the people you'll see, the job you're dreading, the tired end of it, and don't fix any of it. If you pray, say a Hail Mary and the motto's two words, totus tuus; if not, simply hold the day loosely, as something given.
